questions.problem:
Find the limit at $x=\frac{1}{2}$ of the piecewise function $f(x)$ defined by

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}6x+1\, & \text{ for }\,x\le \frac{1}{2} \\ -4{log}_{2}⁡x\, & \text{ for }\,x>\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Approaching from the left, we have $x<\frac{1}{2},$ so we use the expression $f(x)=6x+1.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(1/2)}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(1/2)}^{-}}(6x+1) \\  & =6\cdot \frac{1}{2}+1 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Now,  approaching from the right, we have $x>\frac{1}{2},$ so we use the expression $f(x)=-4{log}_{2}⁡x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {(1/2)}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {(1/2)}^{+}}-4{log}_{2}⁡x \\  & =-4{log}_{2}⁡\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-4{log}_{2}⁡{2}^{-1} \\  & =-4(-1){log}_{2}⁡2 \\  & =-4(-1) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the left- and right-sided limits are equal to $4,$ we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to (1/2)}f(x)=4.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the limit at $x=-1$ of the piecewise function $f(x)$ defined by

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-\sqrt[3]{x}\, & \text{ for }\,x<-1 \\ -2\, & \text{ for }\,x=-1 \\ x+2\, & \text{ for }\,x>-1.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Approaching from the left, we have $x<-1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=-\sqrt[3]{x}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}-\sqrt[3]{x} \\  & =-\sqrt[3]{-1} \\  & =-(-1) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Approaching from the right, we have $x>-1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=x+2.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-1)^{+}}(x+2) \\  & =-1+2 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the left- and right-sided limits are equal to $1,$ we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -1}f(x)=1.
$$

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-6x} & \text{ for }\,x<-2 \\ {e}^{2+x}+3 & \text{ for }\,x\ge -2.\end{aligned}
$$

${lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}f(x)=$

{{field-2}}
questions.worked_solution:
Approaching from the left, we have $x<-2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}-6x}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}\sqrt{{x}^{2}-6x} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2)^{2}-6(-2)} \\  & =\sqrt{4+12} \\  & =\sqrt{16} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Approaching from the right, we have $x\ge -2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)={e}^{2+x}+3.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}{e}^{2+x}+3 \\  & ={e}^{2+(-2)}+3 \\  & ={e}^{0}+3 \\  & =1+3 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to -{2}^{-}}f(x)={lim}_{x\to -{2}^{+}}f(x)=4.
$$

questions.problem:
Find the limit at $x=3$ for the function

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{3x-1}\, & \text{ for }\,x<3 \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(x\pi )\, & \text{ for }\,x\ge 3.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Approaching from the left, we have $x<3,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\sqrt[3]{3x-1}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}\sqrt[3]{3x-1} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{3\cdot 3-1} \\  & =\sqrt[3]{8} \\  & =2\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Approaching from the right, we have $x>3,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\pi ).$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {3}^{+}}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\pi ) \\  & =-1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the two limits are different, we can conclude that

$$
{lim}_{x\to 3}f(x)=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.problem:
Find ${lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}f(x)$ for the function given by

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}-x & \text{ for }\,x<-2 \\ x & \text{ for }\,x>3.\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Approaching $x=-2$ from the left, we have $x<-2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=-x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to (-2)^{-}}(-x) \\  & =-(-2) \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the left-sided limit ${lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}f(x)$ does not exist since $f(x)$ is not defined on the interval $x\in [-2,3].$ 

Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {3}^{-}}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{+}}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to \,{0}^{-}}f(x)$ for the function given by

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sec}⁡x & \text{ for }\,-\frac{\pi }{2}<x<0 \\ \operatorname{csc}⁡x & \text{ for }\,\frac{\pi }{2}<x<\pi \end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The right-sided limit ${lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)$ does not exist since $f(x)$ is not defined on the interval $x\in (0,\frac{\pi }{2}).$ 

Consequently, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE}.
$$

Approaching $x=0$ from the left, we have $x<0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\operatorname{sec}⁡x.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}\operatorname{sec}⁡x \\  & =\operatorname{sec}⁡0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x)=\text{DNE},\,{lim}_{x\to {0}^{-}}f(x)=1.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
In order for ${lim}_{x\to 2}f(x)$ to be equal to $8,$ the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal to $8.$

- Approaching from the left, we have $x\le 2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=a{x}^{2}+2x-3.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}(a{x}^{2}+2x-3) \\  & =a({2}^{2})+2(2)-3 \\  & =4a+1\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the left-sided limit must be equal to $9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x) & =9 \\ 4a+1 & =9 \\ 4a & =8 \\ a & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>2,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=4x+b.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}(4x+b) \\  & =4(2)+b \\  & =8+b\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the right-sided limit must be equal to $9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x) & =9 \\ 8+b & =9 \\ b & =9-8 \\ b & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

f(x)={\begin{aligned}3{e}^{\,\,sin(x-1)}\, & \text{ for }\,x<1 \\ p{x}^{3}\, & \text{ for }\,x\ge 1\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}

In order for ${lim}_{x\to 1}f(x)$ to be equal to $3,$ the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal to $3.$

- Approaching from the left, we have $x<1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=3{e}^{\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-1)}.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}3{e}^{\,\,sin(x-1)} \\  & =3{e}^{\,\,sin(1-1)} \\  & =3{e}^{\,\,sin(0)} \\  & =3{e}^{0} \\  & =3\,.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=p{x}^{3}.$ We get

$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) \\ p & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Approaching from the right, we have $x>0,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=\sqrt{x}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}\sqrt{x} \\  & =\sqrt{0} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing Limits of Piecewise Functions with a Gap in the Domain
canonical_examples.problem:
Find $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}g(x)$ for the function given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+5}}{3x-7}\, & \text{ for }\,x\le 1 \\ (x-2)^{2}-1\, & \text{ for }\,x\ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute $\lim\limits_{x \to \, 1} g(x),$ we must compute the left and right-sided limits separately.

However, the right-sided limit $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1^+}g(x)$ does not exist since $g(x)$ is not defined in the interval $x\in(1,2).$ 

Consequently, the overall limit does not exist either:

$$
\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}g(x) = \text{DNE}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving for a Constant Such that the Limit of a Piecewise Function Exists
canonical_examples.problem:
For the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)={\begin{aligned}4{x}^{3}-2\, & \text{ for }\,x<1 \\ 3x+b\, & \text{ for }\,x>1\end{aligned},\,\end{aligned}
$$

it is known that $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}f(x)$ exists. What is the value of the constant $b?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
In order for $\lim_\limits{x\rightarrow 1}f(x)$ to exist, the left and right-sided limits must both exist and be equal.

- Approaching from the left, we have $x < 1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)=4x^3-2.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}4{x}^{3}-2 \\  & =4(1)^{3}-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Approaching from the right, we have $x>1,$ so we use the expression $f(x)= 3x+b.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}3x+b \\  & =3(1)+b \\  & =3+b.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the left and right-sided limits must be equal, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {1}^{+}}f(x) \\ 2 & =3+b \\ b & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$
